newsitem.title: SPAIN: SOCCER-HEYNCKES GIVEN JOB OF TAKING REAL BACK TO EUROPEAN GLORY.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-HEYNCKES GIVEN JOB OF TAKING REAL BACK TO EUROPEAN GLORY.

text.p: German coach Jupp Heynckes, the authoritarian and often controversial figure who has taken over at Real Madrid, has inherited the daunting task of landing the European Cup for the first time in more than 30 years.
Heynckes, 52, who signed a two-year contract with Real on Tuesday, will be asked to give the six-times winners their long-overdue first victory in the European Cup since 1966.
Since then Real's considerable success at home has contrasted with a trophy-drought on the European stage, with just two UEFA Cup wins.
But Heynckes is no stranger to the big time.

A prolific striker in a career spent mostly with Borussia Moenchengladbach, he was in the West German team which won the European Championship in 1972 and was in the squad which won the World Cup in 1974, though he did not play in the final.

As a free-scoring left-sided forward, he won the West German league five times and the Cup once. He also won the UEFA Cup in 1975, scoring a hat-trick in the second leg of the final with Twente Enschede of the Netherlands.

Heynckes' managerial career took him back to Borussia Moenchengladbach before moving on to Bayern Munich in 1987 where he won the league twice but failed to bring the European success he had promised.

His spell in Munich was punctuated with disputes involving leading players who resented his authoritarian style of leadership, as well as with club officials who at times found him an uncomfortable personality to deal with.
Heynckes, a charming and quiet-talking man in private, paid the price of being too outspoken in public, attracting an image as somewhat brash and arrogant.
He was fired in 1991 and went to Spain the next year, joining Athletic Bilbao, a club which signs players only from the Basque Country.
Heynckes was not a spectacular success there but did well enough to be mentioned in connection with the Real Madrid job as long ago as 1994.
He stayed two years with Bilbao, went back to Germany for a troubled season with Eintracht Frankfurt -- which saw him quit before the end of the campaign -- and then took up the reins at Tenerife.
There he strengthened his image as a proponent of attacking football and took the team to fifth place last year, equalling the club's best-ever standing in the Spanish first division.
The feat earned Tenerife a coveted UEFA Cup place and the Canary Island supporters were delighted by an unprecedented run to the semifinals.
The memorable 5-3 home win over Italy's Lazio was the sort of high-scoring, open game that characterised Tenerife's European campaign.
But despite beginning the domestic season with a 6-0 victory over Compostela, Tenerife lost their way and ended the league in mid-table.
Heynckes has already said he will have to make changes at Real, a side that was at times tediously efficient under coach Fabio Capello.
The departure of Rafael Alkorta will leave a gap in the centre of defence which will be difficult to fill.

Real president Lorenzo Sanz said on Tuesday that he was interested in signing Spanish international Roberto Rios. Rios's contract with Real Betis stipulates that 2 billion pesetas ($13.7 million) must be paid to free the player from his contract.
Other changes Heynckes wants to make include requiring players to wear club uniform when travelling to away games, a rule which may not endear him to all.
But Heynckes has never courted popularity and is no stranger to conflict.
He fell out with Tenerife officials after openly talking of moving to Real in the past weeks.
Heynckes knows it will be all too easy to fall out with the highly-demanding crowd at the Santiago Bernabeu stadium.
Good results kept Capello in favour. But for many the Italian coach, who lasted just one season before deciding to return to AC Milan, left the job undone.
"I hope Heynckes finishes off my project," said Capello, in a clear reference to winning the European Cup. ($ = 145.6 Spanish Pesetas)
